analysis.answer: The measurement pack did not change the runs. All 5,200 S0 rows (2,800 test and 2,400 band) match their round-2 rows with the same (name, q, seed) on every field the two share, with nothing off even by rounding: 761,642 field comparisons over 159 fields (all_delay, passed, ttc_net, every ttc3/ttc2/ttc15/sev3 split, b3/b45/b7_step, brake_net, b45_net, collisions, teleports, arrived, N, dist, fuel, the lists flow_min, v20_min, lv and pert_log, and the rest). 0 fall only within 1e-9 and 0 differ. The key sets are identical apart from the 53 added m_* pack keys, and each cfg is identical once its added "measure" key is removed. In v5b/, the code difference between round 2 (6c49e7e) and the S0 run (79b889b) is only the pack: measure.py is new and plant_sweep.py gains its hooks. The pack's own sums hold on all 5,560 runs, all 5,560 space-time files are present and well formed, summary_rows_*.json recompute exactly from the rows, and report_rows_*.txt regenerate line for line. S1 is complete and clean: 360 rows = 9 arms x 2 levels x 20 seeds, seeds exactly 7,440,900-919, no duplicates. Those seeds appear nowhere else under v5b1_runs except the S1 smoke files. S1 had 0 collisions, 0 teleports and 0 contact steps. Low finished_pct at 7,000 (54-70 %) looks built-in, not a failure: even free-flowing 3,500 finishes only 84-86 %, and all_delay counts unfinished and queued vehicles. Two things matter when reading the results. First, os1_15_10 and p333 are the same runs on all 20 S1 seeds at 3,500, and on 17/10/6/1 of 20 band seeds at 4,500/5,000/5,250/5,500; this follows from the rules' definitions. Second, p333's 0.934 'longest level' share has a likely cause in the code: levels step up one at a time, at most once per 10-s hold, after a vehicle enters. The arm mapping holds: d0u500-d4u500 is baseline-v3 (baseline_v3/conf3/train/C{i}_u500.pt), and the S0 job configs equal round 2's for all 70 test and 24 band arms.

findings.statement: The statistic in use, common1.effect/raw (from docs/research/conf3/common.py), implements the stated convention. Two details matter: its default CI is not 95 %, and its denominator is held fixed.

Missing counters read as 0 (val). Bootstrap: np.random.default_rng(20261104), 20,000 resamples of seeds, percentiles pct with default (1.25, 98.75), i.e. 97.5 % two-sided; a 95 % CI needs pct=(2.5, 97.5) (decide2.P95). effect() = raw() rounded to 0.1. arm_mean = per-seed mean over the learners of every numeric key on the intersection of their seeds.
findings.method: Code reading.

caveats: comparisons_made = 0 statistical comparisons; no effect or CI was computed in this area. The integrity checks were exact equality tests: 761,642 field comparisons between S0 and round-2 rows, plus checks of the pack's own sums, the summary files and the configs.
Exact equality shows the pack did not change the S0 runs on code 79b889b. It does not show that the plant or the metrics are correct.

Which machine produced the round-2 stored rows is not recorded here, so I cannot say whether the S0-vs-round-2 match is also a cross-machine match. That s01_smoke1/2 and round2_measure_smoke_2354 ran on the local machine is inferred from folder names.
S1 has no stored reference. Its reproducibility rests on 3 repeated runs (seed 7,440,900 only) and on the pack checks passing.

The explanations for finished_pct (built-in floor from the 1,500-s window) and for p333's 0.934 (one-level steps once per 10-s hold) come from code and data patterns. I did not trace them vehicle by vehicle.
The zgrep scan of the .jsonl.gz files ran with errors suppressed. It printed no match, but a read error would also print nothing.
S1's 3,500 level has only 8 distinct arms (os1_15_10 = p333 on all 20 seeds). Any S1 reading that counts them as two opponents double-counts.
X2's duration (180 s) is the upper bound of the training draw (uniform 60-180 s). 'Inside the draw' holds only at the boundary of its range.

analysis.area: x1_exposure: why v3w has more close-following (ttc_net) than no control in X1 but not in X2
analysis.answer: The exposure hypothesis does not explain v3w's X1 excess. In that hypothesis, no control's stopped queues hide its close-following and v3w turns them into moving dense traffic. Per unit of exposure, v3w's close-following stays higher than no control's: 13.8 % more per vehicle-km [3.9, 22.3], 24 % more per vehicle-second at 18 km/h or faster [13, 30], and 9.9 % more per vehicle served [0.7, 20.3]. v3w has less exposure in the risky states: 45 % less vehicle-time below 18 km/h, 24 % less at 18-36 km/h and 8 % lower density in moving cells. In a speed-band decomposition, the exposure part is -648 TTC-s per run [-704, -594] and the rate part is +873 [778, 966], netting +224 [119, 328]. The excess sits on merge 2's acceleration section 4a (+272 [229, 312]) and on edge 3 (+139 [88, 189]), partly offset by fewer on ramp 2 (-113) and the remaining roads (-73). In time, it falls in the recovery windows: 'rest' +161 [86, 232] and 'after' +59 [37, 81], and not before or during the slowdowns. On 4a, the largest part, v3w has the same jam as no control and 5 % more moving vehicle-time, so no stopped queue is being replaced there. Exposure may contribute only on edge 3, where v3w replaces no control's long-lasting spill-back queue with moving traffic. X2 differs mainly by an offset: v3w adds close-following outside merge 1 in both cells (out_E30 +308 in X1, +217 in X2). But in X2 no control's queue reaches merge 1 (E30 median 456 against 61 in X1), and v3w removes most of it (-288 [-379, -202]). That cancels the addition. The per-exposure increase also exists in X2 (rate part +401 [320, 484]), but there it is confined to traffic below 18 km/h. My best reading is that v3w follows more closely at small closing speeds: the required-deceleration count (sev3) is unchanged and the excess is larger at the 1.5 and 2 s thresholds. That reading is an inference: no TTC event was traced. Everything here is descriptive and report-only.

findings.statement: Definitions, read from the code. ttc_net = E30 + out_E30, computed in b_env._second via _merge_stats and _net_stats. At each 1-s sample after the 300-s warm-up (1,500 samples), it counts the vehicles that meet all of these: (1) anywhere on the network, all classes (car, ALKS, truck), ramps and junction lanes included; (2) a same-lane leader within 200 m (libsumo getLeader); (3) a positive closing speed dv = v_f - v_lead > 0; (4) bumper gap (lead[1] + minGap) / dv < 3.0 s (TTC_REWARD). The unit is vehicle-seconds. A stopped follower cannot count; a creeping follower behind a slower leader can. E30 covers only the merge-1 area (lane 2_0 tail, 3a_0, 3a_1, 3_0 head); out_E30 is the rest of the network. ttc3 (plant_sweep.conflicts) uses the same criterion at the same instant and equals ttc_net in all 2,800 rows. Splits: road '3', '4a', 'ramp2' (r2, rj2), 'rest' (1, 2, 3a, 4, 5, r, rj and internal lanes); follower speed lo < 5 m/s, mid 5-10, hi >= 10; period by absolute time. X1 periods: before < 600 s, taper 600-620 and 1200-1220, hold to 720 and 1320, after to 840 and 1440, rest the remainder. X2: before < 700, taper 700-720, hold to 880, after to 1000, rest to 1800. ttc2 and ttc15 use 2 and 1.5 s thresholds; sev3 counts dv^2 / (2 max(gap, 0.1)) >= 3 m/s^2.

caveats: No TTC event was traced. The stored data has no per-event record and running simulations was not allowed. The 'shorter gaps at small closing speeds' mechanism is an inference from the counters: sev3 unchanged, larger relative excess at 1.5 and 2 s, higher rates in every band. A traced re-run of a few X1 seeds (for example 7,440,853, 7,440,878 and median seeds 7,440,854 and 7,440,869) would show follower class, tau, gap and dv per sample. Per the project lesson, its untraced counters must be compared to show the trace changes nothing.
The splits are marginal (road, speed band and period separately), not joint, so I cannot say which speed band the 4a excess falls in, or which period the edge-3 excess falls in.

Band exposures come from 5-km/h step histograms, with the 15-20 and 35-40 km/h bins split uniformly. Edge and period exposures come from the mainline space-time field (cell mean speed; ramps excluded; 92-98 % of vehicle-seconds), while the TTC counts include ramps.

The no-control-calibrated regressions are model-based. v3w's jam share (0.087-0.205) lies partly below no control's range (0.145-0.375), so they extrapolate. The X2 band model has a negative hi-band coefficient. Use them only as corroboration of the Kitagawa result.
The 'rest' road group lumps edges 1, 2, 3a, 4, 5, ramp 1 and junction lanes. The X2 offset is placed at merge 1 through the separate E30 counter (merge-1 lanes), not through the road split.
The X1-X2 contrast pairs runs by seed number. I assume, without checking, that the same seed gives the same demand realisation in both cells; an unpaired comparison would widen the CIs.

Per-seed correlations of paired differences are confounded by the shared no-control run and seed; even the shuffled-nc null is only an approximate null, because pairing also carries seed-level co-movement.

About 2,870 CIs and tests were computed (results.json 1,504; deeper.json 1,164; third.json 180; merge1.json 20), most of them descriptive. None is corrected for multiplicity; 'CI excludes 0' is the only strength statement used. Nothing here supports a thesis claim.

verify.answer_verdict: Every number I re-derived matches the analyst's exactly, using my own code and the same statistic and bootstrap. The statement 'v3w's close-following per unit of exposure is higher than no control's in X1' holds under every network-level normalisation I tried. Those include per vehicle-km, per vehicle-second, per moving vehicle-second, per vehicle served and per speed band, and also a speed-drop (approach) exposure from the space-time fields: TTC per app20 is -37.6 % [-43.8, -17.3]. Two parts of the answer should change. (1) The 'best reading', shorter gaps at small closing speeds and low required deceleration with the severity count unchanged, is contradicted by road-level counters. Where the excess sits, severe closings rise: sev3_r_4a +12.7 [8.2, 17.2] on nc's median 18, and edge 3 +3.5 [2.8, 4.2]. The network total stays flat only because ramp 2 (-11.0) and 'rest' (-3.3) fall. On 4a the relative excess is similar at all thresholds, and hard-braking events are up about 25 %. Harder approaches to the slowdown queue tail or to lane-end stops on the acceleration lane are at least as consistent. (2) Exposure is ruled out only in the narrow 'stopped queues hide TTC' sense. For 4a, the largest component, the result depends on the exposure measure. Per moving vehicle-second, v3w's rate is about 37 % higher. Per approach exposure, which roughly doubles under v3w because traffic now arrives at speed from a free-flowing edge 3, its rate is 20 % lower. That proxy is not validated on 4a, so neither reading is established. The edge-3 part is a rate effect under both measures. Further wording fixes: on 4a v3w has 11 % less jam [3.9, 18.8], not the same jam. The within-arm jam-TTC correlation is confounded with traffic volume (rho jam/vs 0.94), so it cannot show that queues cause close-following. The X2 per-exposure increase is mostly, not only, below 18 km/h. The X2 offset explanation (no control's merge-1 queue, removed by v3w) holds, and its seed-pairing assumption is now verified. Revised summary: the mechanism is not identified. A rate increase is present network-wide and on edge 3. The 4a excess may come from exposure to queue-tail approaches and lane-end merge stops. A traced re-run is still needed. Report-only; about 1,440 descriptive CIs computed, none corrected for multiplicity.

analysis.area: x1_braking: hard braking in X1 (and X2), v3w / tail / sw / baseline-v3 against nc, 3E-T, 3E-X1/X2, p333, os1_15_10
analysis.answer: The lead's X1 numbers are reproduced: events_ge45 medians are v3w 1,044, nc 818.5 and 3E-T 868.5 (v3w minus nc +204 [149, 267]), and car cascade share is 0.227 vs 0.203. That count does not measure hard braking, though. The -4.5 m/s2 threshold is exactly the normal maximum deceleration of human cars and ALKS (SUMO default decel 4.5). Car steps pile up just below -4.5 and almost never go past -5.0 (558 vs 2 steps per run). By IEEE arithmetic on SUMO's update formula, a step braking at that limit reads below -4.5 only at about 7-29 km/h. So events_ge45 mostly counts limit braking that passes through low speed. Two counts do not depend on which side of -4.5 a step lands. Events peaking at -4.0 or harder rise only about 8 % for v3w vs nc (+343 [230, 497] in X1, +341 in X2), about 5-6 % per km in both classes. Events past the normal limit (-5 to -9 m/s2) are ALKS-only and about five times nc's: 48 vs 9 per run, +38 [37, 40], the same in X1 and X2. Every short-headway controller shows this, and v3w has the fewest of them (3E-T 51.5, p333 77, os1_15_10 89.5). The X1-specific gap comes mostly from nc's count dropping in X1 vs X2 (-141 [-260, -67] at unchanged -4.0 count), less from v3w rising (+49 [23, 88]). Exposure explains little: per vehicle-km the -4.5 excess is still +22 %, per vehicle served +19 %. Braking is not stored by time or place. The speed fields suggest the extra limit braking sits at sharper speed fronts at the merge-2 section 4a, mostly outside the slowdown windows: v3w runs edge 3 at 48-73 km/h into a short congested 4a, where nc's queue spills back. My best but uncertain reading of what v3w's ALKS do differently: they hold shorter headways (mean level 2.2 on edge 3 and 1.6 on 4a, vs 3E-T's 1.45 and 1.10). That buys flow but costs some braking past the limit by the ALKS themselves, plus slightly more limit braking by everyone near the merge-2 bottleneck. The cascade-share rise holds against nc (car +0.025 [0.007, 0.032]) but not against 3E-T, and has no proper null. It should not be read as stronger wave propagation.

findings.statement: Definitions (from the code). A braking event starts at the first 0.1-s step with getAcceleration <= -3.0 m/s2 after the warm-up and ends at the first step above -3.0, or at run end. Its peak is the minimum acceleration. Peak bin i covers (edge i+1, edge i] of PEAK_EDGES (-3, -3.5, -4, -4.5, -5, -6, -7, -8, -9, -100), so events_ge45_<class> = bins 3+ (peak <= -4.5). A cascade: when a follower's event starts, its leader (getLeader within 200 m) began its latest event 0-3 s earlier; it is counted in the follower's class. Cascade share = m_cascade_c / m_events_c. b3_step, b45_step and b7_step are the seconds with a <= -3, -4.5 and -7, all vehicles; alks_* is the same for ALKS only. free_brake_alks_step is ALKS seconds at a <= -3 with no leader within 200 m or a gap/speed above 3 s. Classes: car = human Krauss, alks = every automated car (SUMO ACC model, decel 4.5, emergencyDecel 9, action step 0.5 s), truck.

analysis.answer: The 0.934 for p333 is measured correctly, but the panel's title has the gap backwards. level_share_on[-1] is level index 3, and HEADWAYS_S = (1.6, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8) s, so index 3 is 0.8 s, the shortest gap, not the longest. p333 is CavRule([3,3,3]): it asks for 0.8 s for every ALKS in every zone (want share 1.000, 0 reversals, 0 excess changes). The missing ~6.6 % is the start-up climb: every ALKS starts at level 0 (1.6 s) and moves up one level per 10-s hold, which takes about 10.5 s of its ~159 s with V2V on in X1. That is why the share rises with demand, from 0.910 at 3,500 to 0.947 at 7,000. In X1, v3w shows no sign of acting out of distribution. Paired with X2 (same seeds, same mean density), its confidence (+0.004 [-0.005, +0.012]) and reversal share (+0.002 [-0.005, +0.005]) are unchanged, and its entropy is slightly lower. Only sw is less confident in X1. v3w does not pick shorter gaps in X1; it picks longer ones. Its share at 0.8 s is -0.044 [-0.057, -0.035] against X2 and -0.057 against band runs of the same density. The pack stores no decision time series, so the timing comes from a proxy: ALKS grouped by departure time, rebuilt exactly from the seed. It suggests v3w lengthens its gaps for vehicles passing both slowdowns, including the second one (the out-of-draw part), and keeps them somewhat longer afterwards.

caveats: Report-only and descriptive. About 1,250 interval estimates without multiplicity control (163 paired X1-X2, 90 density residuals, 104 cross-arm, 144 period/road, 750 cohort bins, plus 2 validation), so some 95 % CIs excluding 0 are expected by chance. The inverted label in D1 affects any reading of the 'longest level' panels, including the lead's first look: a high value means more time at the SHORTEST gap (0.8 s).

X1 is outside v3w's training draw mainly because it has TWO slowdowns. Each one alone (edge 4, 25 km/h, 120 s, start 600 or 1,200 s) sits at the edges of the draw's ranges (25-60 km/h, 60-180 s, start in [400, 1200)). The time structure (D9) is a proxy. Per-vehicle records are whole-trip totals. Edge-passage times come from a pooled-lane speed field and ignore insertion delay and lanes. The first-slowdown X1-X2 contrast is confounded by X2's own slowdown, which hits the same cohorts.

The density-matched fits are band quadratics in mean mainline density, which misses where congestion sits. S1 values are extrapolations. Confidence is binned in tenths and interpolated (measure.quantiles). tail's confidence comes from its 6-checkpoint averaged distribution, and sw's covers only its policy part (from x_from = 594.72 m past the start of 3a). ttc_net/ttc3 count TTC < 3 s for all vehicles, humans included, so they do not measure ALKS gaps directly. analysis.answer: "p333 wins everywhere" is wrong against v3w, and against tail and sw too. Across 9 settings and 6 metrics (54 paired comparisons), v3w is better than p333 with the 95 % CI excluding 0 in 25 and tied in 28. p333 is better in only 1: finished_pct at 5,000, by -0.19 percentage points [-0.32, -0.05]. On delay, p333 never beats v3w with the CI excluding 0. v3w has less delay in X1 (+5.5 % [+2.9, +8.0]), in X2 (+6.1 [+3.4, +7.4]) and at 7,000 (+3.7 [+2.6, +5.2]). They tie at 3,500, 4,500, 5,000, 5,250, 5,500 and 6,000, although p333's point estimates are slightly lower at 3,500, 4,500, 5,000 and 5,500. On close-following (ttc_net), v3w has 40-47 % less than p333 in X1, X2 and at 5,500, 6,000 and 7,000, with matching gains on b3_step, b45_step and flow there. From 3,500 to 5,250 the two tie, with very wide CIs. The claim is only partly right in two narrow senses. Among the rules, p333 has the lowest delay: it beats 3E-T at 3,500, 4,500, 5,250 and 5,500, and it is identical to os1_15_10 on most low-demand seeds (20/20 at 3,500, 17/20 at 4,500). But it has the most close-following and hard braking of all rules at 5,300 and above. Also, the unpaired ASCII panel medians at 5,000 favour p333 on 12 of 16 panels, but paired only 3 of those 16 differ, all small. a) The claim "every controller has far more close-following than no control" holds at 7,000 for all four controllers, both per run and per vehicle-km. No control's base there is 2,424 samples per run (0.179 per vehicle-km). For v3w the excess is +1,706 per run and +61 % per vehicle-km.
